How Long Does a WordPress to Webflow Migration Take?

PublishedSeptember 15, 2026
Last updatedSeptember 15, 2026
AuthorFionn LennonFounder, Legency Media
Share
On this page
Section

A WordPress to Webflow migration for a typical B2B marketing site is a four to eight week project. The honest answer under that headline is that four factors set your position in that window, and you can price your own timeline in ten minutes by walking through them. This piece is the walkthrough.

It pairs with our step-by-step migration guide, which covers how to move without losing rankings. This one covers how long the move takes and why.

The four factors that set the timeline

Unique page designs, counted properly. Template count drives the build time, and copies of a design cost almost nothing. A site with 200 URLs is often 12 unique layouts plus a blog template, and that builds faster than a 40-URL site where every page was art-directed by hand. Count your templates before you count anything else.

Content structure. Every WordPress post type becomes a Webflow CMS collection: blog, case studies, team, events. A clean export maps across quickly. The time sink is content that lives inside page builders like Elementor or WPBakery, because it exports as markup soup and gets rebuilt by hand.

Design intent. Rebuilding the current design as it stands is the fast lane. A redesign during the move is a legitimate choice and it is a second project sharing the same deadline: scope it as one.

The SEO carryover. Redirect mapping, metadata transfer, schema rebuilds and the launch checklist protect the rankings you spent years earning. This work runs alongside the build rather than after it, and skipping it is how migrations end up cheap and costly at the same time.

The week-by-week shape

For that typical B2B marketing site, the shape we scope is: week one for the audit, redirect map and CMS architecture. Weeks two to four for the build, with content migrating into collections as templates finish. Week five for the SEO carryover checks, QA on staging and client review. Launch sits at the start of week six, held deliberately for a low-traffic day, with a post-launch monitoring week after it.

Small sites compress the middle. A 10-page site with one blog collection and no builder debris is a two-week project. What stretches a timeline is rarely size alone: it is builder-locked content, missing access to the old site, or a redesign discovered mid-project.

What you can do to shorten it

  1. Get access sorted before day one. WordPress admin, hosting, DNS and analytics access delays are the most common dead week in any migration.
  2. Freeze the old site’s content two weeks before launch. Every post published on the old site during the build adds a migration and redirect task at the worst time.
  3. Decide rebuild versus redesign in writing, up front. Mid-project design changes are the single biggest timeline risk we see.
  4. Assign one approver. Staging review by committee adds a week for every voice in the room.

The platform decision itself, including who maintains what after launch, is covered in Webflow vs WordPress for B2B marketing teams. What a migration includes when we run one is on the WordPress migration service page.

Frequently asked questions

Can a WordPress to Webflow migration be done in a week?

A small brochure site with no CMS content can move in a week when access is ready on day one. A site with a blog, redirects and traffic worth protecting deserves the full schedule, because the SEO carryover work needs its own days.

Does the old site stay live during the migration?

Yes. The build happens on a Webflow staging domain while the WordPress site serves visitors as normal, and the switch is a DNS change at launch.

When does traffic recover after the switch?

With a complete redirect map and matching metadata, rankings typically hold rather than dip, and crawl activity settles within a few weeks. The migration guide covers the checks that make that the expected outcome.

What does a migration cost?

Cost follows the same four factors as the timeline, which is why we quote from a template count and a content audit rather than a raw page count. The service page explains what a scoped quote includes.
